Harmonic Progression: Practice for Chapter 9

Exercises for Chapter 9 of Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom: the circle of fifths progression and its pieces (ii–V–I, I–vi–ii–V …), harmonic rhythm, the four harmonic functions, ♭VII in popular music, the best-seller I–V–vi–IV and i–VII–VI–VII, with the book’s listening examples.

This page goes with Chapter 9, Harmonic Progression and Harmonic Function of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. It builds on Chapter 7, Roman Numerals and Chapter 8, Seventh Chords.

This chapter is about chords in order, so most of the practice here is listening. The drills play each progression on the piano (or show it, or both); the clips are the book’s own, cut where the book cuts them. Every drill has Settings, and is also on the Theory Drills page.

Typing a progression: the chords in order with spaces between them: I vi IV V. Case is the quality, as before. Type b or ♭ before a numeral for ♭VII. With Answer with: lead-sheet symbols, type C Am F G (a small letter is minor here too).

9.1 The circle of fifths progression

Each chord’s root is a fifth above the next one’s (or a fourth below): I IV vii° iii vi ii V I in major, i iv VII III VI ii° V i in minor, with only the notes of the key, so one fifth (IV to vii°) is diminished. The bass makes a sequence: a short idea repeated at a lower pitch, which is why the progression sounds so inevitable. Read 9.1 · Open Music Theory: Diatonic Sequences

The book’s exercise 1 writes the circle on paper, in F major and B minor. This drill asks for the same chords as lead-sheet symbols:

NoteListen: the book’s circle of fifths examples, Baroque to 2010s

9.2 Harmonic rhythm

Harmonic rhythm is how long each chord lasts: a chord a bar in “Fly Me to the Moon” and “I Will Survive”, two chords a bar in the Mozart and Wagner. It can change inside a song: in “Pompeii” it doubles, from four beats a chord to two. Read 9.2

9.3 Shorter progressions from the circle

Pieces of the circle are everywhere, especially in jazz standards and pop: ii–V–I; vi–ii–V–I and its rotations I–vi–ii–V and ii–V–I–vi; iii–vi–ii–V, often looped, and its rotation ii–V–iii–vi. Read 9.3

By ear only. Turn on Sound only for ear training, or use this one:

NoteMore of the book’s examples

9.4 Harmonic function

A chord’s function is what it tends to do next. The book uses four:

Function Major Minor Tends to
Tonic (ton.) I i rest; can go anywhere
Tonic prolongation (ton. prol.) iii, vi III, VI move on to a pre-dominant
Pre-dominant (pre-dom.) IV, ii iv, ii° move on to a dominant
Dominant (dom.) V, vii° V, vii° go to the tonic

In minor, VII (the subtonic) has one job: it leads to III. Two exceptions: IV has tonic prolongation function when it goes straight to I (the plagal cadence), and I/5th has dominant function when it goes to V. The deceptive cadence (V–vi) is the other exception to the flowchart. Read 9.4 · Open Music Theory: Introduction to Harmony

9.5 Exceptions created by sequences

When a progression breaks the flowchart, look for a sequence: a pattern of chords repeated a step or more lower or higher, which takes the chords wherever the pattern goes. The book’s examples are “Flashdance… What a Feeling” (the book’s clip of it is no longer on YouTube) and the verse of “Hotel California”: Read 9.5

9.6 ♭VII in popular music

In rock and pop, ♭VII (a major chord on the lowered 7th, B♭ in C major) is everywhere. It can come before tonic, pre-dominant or dominant chords, so it can stand in for any function except tonic, and ♭VII–IV–I is a common way to end a phrase. Read 9.6 · Open Music Theory: Modal Schemas

NoteListen: the book’s ♭VII examples

9.7 The best-seller progression

I–V–vi–IV is in so many hit songs that it has its own name, and its rotations vi–IV–I–V and IV–I–V–vi are just as common. vi–IV–I–V can also be heard in the relative minor as i–VI–III–VII: which one you hear depends on which chord feels like home. Read 9.7 · Open Music Theory: Four-Chord Schemas

Listen: which rotation?

9.8 i–VII–VI–VII

i–VII–VI–VII (Am G F G) walks the bass down from the tonic, like the flamenco “Andalusian” progression (Am G F E) but turning back up at the end. It also comes rotated as VI–VII–i–VII, or VI–VII–i–i. In the relative major it is vi–V–IV–V. Read 9.8

NoteListen: the book’s examples

NoteFor teachers
  • Links with your settings: open a drill’s Settings, then Copy a link with these settings. Add &lock=1 for a test, &count=20 for a score.
  • Progressions drilled: the circle of fifths in major and minor and its pieces (ii–V–I, vi–ii–V–I, I–vi–ii–V, ii–V–I–vi, iii–vi–ii–V, ii–V–iii–vi); I–V–I, i–V–i, I–ii–V–I, I–IV–V–I, i–iv–V–i, I–vi–IV–V and IV–V–I–vi; I–V–vi–IV and its two rotations, I–♭VII–IV–I, i–VII–VI–VII, VI–VII–i–VII and VI–VII–i–i.
  • Voicing: the drills play root-position triads (bass root, close chord above), two a bar. They are for hearing the bass and the qualities, not for voice leading, which the book takes up later.
  • Function drill: root-position diatonic triads only. VII in minor is left out (the book gives it no function of its own), and the two exceptions (IV–I, I/5th–V) need context, so they are taught in the text, not drilled.
  • Videos: the clips use the book’s YouTube links and start and end times; each title was checked against YouTube. “Flashdance… What a Feeling” is no longer available there, so it is left out.
